title: A highly protective, durable and readily deliverable malaria vaccine

concept.text: The proposed innovation is a malaria vaccine that combines strong protection with sustained benefit and a delivery schedule practical for widespread use in endemic settings, including among young children. Its defining achievement would be the combination of protection, durability and deliverability across varied parasite populations and exposure histories. Lifelong immunity after one dose would be exceptionally valuable, but is not a prerequisite for this concept. This is the proposed capability, not an achievement established by the supplied evidence.

Three outcomes must remain distinct: preventing infection, preventing severe disease in someone who becomes infected, and reducing onward transmission. Sterile protection means preventing an infection from becoming established under the conditions tested; it does not by itself demonstrate lifelong protection or population-level interruption of transmission. A convincing account of this vaccine would specify which outcomes it achieves and how long each benefit lasts.

significance.text: As a conditional impact argument, strong and sustained protection delivered through a manageable vaccination schedule could substantially reduce malaria illness and deaths. Practical delivery is integral to that potential: a highly protective intervention would have less public-health reach if its administration, repeat dosing or supply requirements prevented broad use. Protection in young children and across endemic settings would therefore matter alongside performance under controlled experimental conditions.

If the vaccine also substantially reduced transmission, it could support elimination alongside vector control, treatment and surveillance. That possibility requires separate evidence: individual protection against severe disease does not establish an effect on transmission, and even demonstrated infection prevention would not alone establish that elimination is achievable in every setting. These are reasoned potential consequences, not demonstrated outcomes or predictions from the supplied trial report.

missing_breakthrough.text: The central unresolved capability is to combine broad, durable protection with practical delivery. As a synthesis of the proposed goal, the scientific challenge is to establish protection that persists despite differences in parasite strains, prior exposure, age and endemic setting. Strong protection shortly after vaccination against a matching experimental challenge would leave open whether protection survives longer intervals, different parasites and repeated natural exposure.

The engineering challenge is to turn a protective biological approach into a consistently manufactured and readily administered product. For the reported genetically attenuated parasite approach, proposed development questions include whether attenuation reliably preserves safety while eliciting protection, whether doses can be produced consistently, and whether a practical delivery method can reproduce protection reported after mosquito-bite administration. These are development questions inferred from the concept and reported approach; the retained source does not document their solutions.

A further challenge is to establish the relationship among infection prevention, severe-disease prevention and transmission reduction. Each requires suitable measurements and study designs. A controlled infection experiment can investigate protection under defined conditions, while durability, safety across relevant populations and community transmission effects require broader and longer observation.

current_state.text: The supplied research identifies a study attributed to Roozen and colleagues, titled “Single immunization with genetically attenuated Pf∆mei2 (GA2) parasites by mosquito bite in controlled human malaria infection: a placebo-controlled randomized trial,” and gives a Nature Medicine publication date of 3 January 2025. It reports sterile protection in nine of ten participants after one immunization through 50 mosquitoes carrying genetically attenuated parasites, compared with none of five controls, following a matching parasite challenge six weeks later. These details are preserved as a reported research lead; they cannot be independently confirmed from the retained source material supplied for this record.

The evidence review found that the retained PubMed artifact contains only a cookie-access message, with no article-specific abstract or results. It therefore cannot verify the article identity, participant counts, protection result, challenge matching or six-week interval. The earlier research also reports failed access to the publisher and a full-text mirror, but its statement that the abstract was inspected is not substantiated by the retained artifact. This is an access and verification limitation, not evidence that the reported result is false.

Even if the reported findings are confirmed, their stated scope is a small controlled human infection experiment with a short follow-up interval and a matching parasite challenge. Such a result would not establish durable protection under natural exposure, effectiveness against diverse parasites, protection against severe disease, safety and effectiveness in young children, community transmission reduction or a deployable vaccination method. No bounded search record was supplied to establish currency through 1 November 2026, so this record cannot claim to represent the latest state of malaria vaccine development or provide a comprehensive comparison with other vaccines.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: large trials across multiple endemic settings would show strong protection against infection and severe disease after a practical vaccination schedule, with safety evaluated across the relevant populations, including young children. Protocols would need to define acceptable protection, duration, dosing burden and safety outcomes in advance. These are proposed evaluation dimensions, not established numerical standards, and the supplied material does not resolve appropriate thresholds.
completion_criteria.label: Strong protection against infection and severe disease after practical schedules

completion_criteria.text: Follow-up would measure waning protection over a prespecified, practically meaningful interval and assess performance across parasite strains, exposure histories and settings. Independent replication and consistent findings across sites would strengthen confidence. Finite studies would establish the demonstrated breadth and duration of protection; they would not prove literal universality or lifelong immunity.
completion_criteria.label: Follow-up establishes waning protection and demonstrated breadth across populations

completion_criteria.text: Practical completion would also require reproducible manufacturing and administration, with evidence that the deliverable product retains the protection observed in research. The dosing schedule, need for boosters, storage and distribution requirements, and delivery resources should be explicit. For the reported mosquito-delivered approach, a convincing deployment claim would require evidence for an operationally practical administration method.
completion_criteria.label: Reproducible manufacturing and practical administration retain demonstrated vaccine protection

completion_criteria.text: If transmission reduction forms part of the claimed breakthrough, community studies would need to measure that effect separately from individual protection and account for concurrent vector control, treatment and surveillance. A vaccine could meet a major disease-prevention objective without establishing transmission interruption; any elimination claim would require additional evidence appropriate to the setting.
completion_criteria.label: Community studies measure claimed transmission reduction accounting for concurrent interventions

related_concepts.text: INF-04, “A reliable way to break malaria transmission through its vectors,” shares the malaria-control and potential elimination objective. INF-13 acts through vaccination of people, while INF-04 targets the vector route. Their effects could be complementary, but success in one does not establish success in the other, and the entries retain distinct completion requirements.

INF-03, “A tuberculosis vaccine that interrupts transmission,” overlaps in the need to distinguish individual protection from population-level transmission effects. INF-01, “A broadly protective HIV vaccine,” and INF-08, “A pre-emptive vaccine against diverse pandemic coronaviruses,” share the challenge of protection across pathogen diversity. These are conceptual parallels; evidence of breadth or durability for one pathogen does not transfer directly to another.

INF-09, “A rapid, end-to-end vaccine response to a newly identified pathogen,” overlaps in manufacturing and delivery capabilities, but emphasizes response speed. INF-13 instead centers on the sustained protective performance and practical use of a malaria vaccine. INF-05, “Near-patient diagnosis of the cause and treatability of most serious infections,” concerns a complementary diagnostic capability rather than preventive immunity; better diagnosis would not substitute for vaccine protection.

unresolved_issues: The cited article's identity, bibliographic details, numerical findings, challenge conditions and follow-up interval remain unverified from the retained artifact.
The discrepancy between the research statement that the abstract was inspected and the retained cookie-access message remains unresolved.
No bounded search record establishes currency through 1 November 2026 or supports a comprehensive account of other malaria vaccines.
The supplied evidence does not resolve long-term protection, parasite-strain breadth, performance in young children, severe-disease prevention, transmission effects or practical delivery.
Operational thresholds for strong protection, sufficient durability, acceptable safety and a practical schedule remain to be defined.
The broader scientific framing and conditional public-health impact lack usable supporting source text in this evidence package; they are retained as explicit synthesis and proposals.

brief.title: Lasting malaria protection with practical vaccination
possible: Families in places where malaria is common could gain strong, lasting protection through a vaccination schedule that health services can deliver widely, including to young children.
why: Sustained protection could reduce malaria illness and deaths. A manageable schedule would help that protection reach more people.
A vaccine that also reduced the spread of malaria could support elimination alongside mosquito control, treatment and disease monitoring.

sources.who: Geert V T Roozen and colleagues
sources.showed: In a small randomized trial, most vaccinated participants resisted infection after deliberate exposure to closely matched parasites. Mosquito bites delivered parasites weakened by genetic changes.
sources.quote: Here we report the safe administration of GA2-MB with no breakthrough malaria
sources.cited_for: This trial supports strong short-term protection against infection after a single vaccination.
sources.not_established: It does not establish lasting protection under natural exposure, effectiveness in young children or practical delivery.

sources.showed: Long-term follow-up of children given the RTS,S/AS01 malaria vaccine found waning protection. Older vaccinated children had more malaria illness than controls at one site, without evidence of a rebound in severe disease.
sources.quote:
Vaccine efficacy of three or four RTS,S/AS01 doses against severe 
and clinical malaria decreased over time in both age categories.
sources.cited_for: Long follow-up can reveal fading protection and differences between settings.
sources.not_established: These findings do not establish how long protection from genetically weakened parasites would last.

sources.showed: A small trial in adults who had never had malaria found strong protection after repeated vaccination through mosquito bites carrying genetically weakened parasites.
sources.quote: Adverse events were similar across the trial groups.
sources.cited_for: This trial supports the protective potential of parasites engineered to stop developing late in the liver.
sources.not_established: It does not establish lasting protection against varied parasites, effectiveness in children or a practical vaccination method.

shown: Roozen and colleagues prevented infection in 90% of vaccinated participants in a small controlled trial. Vaccination used mosquito bites carrying genetically weakened parasites. Participants faced closely matched parasites weeks later, so the result establishes short-term protection under controlled conditions.
missing: Large trials have yet to establish strong protection against infection and severe disease, with acceptable safety, including in young children.
Protection must last under repeated natural exposure and work across parasite strains, prior exposure histories and settings.
Consistent manufacturing and practical administration must preserve the protection achieved with mosquito-bite vaccination.
Community studies must establish any claimed reduction in the spread of malaria separately from protection of vaccinated people.

milestones.label: Strong protection with a practical vaccination schedule
milestones.explanation: Large trials across places where malaria is common would have to show safe, strong protection against infection and severe disease, including in young children. This would establish benefit with a usable schedule.

milestones.label: Follow-up establishes lasting protection across populations and parasites
milestones.explanation: Follow-up would have to measure fading protection and performance across parasite strains, exposure histories and settings. Consistent, independently repeated findings would establish how broadly and how long protection holds.

milestones.label: Consistent production and practical delivery preserve protection
milestones.explanation: A consistently manufactured vaccine would have to retain protection through practical administration, with dosing, storage and delivery needs defined. This would connect experimental success to widespread use.

milestones.label: Community studies establish any claimed reduction in spread
milestones.explanation: Any claim of reduced spread would require community studies accounting for mosquito control, treatment and monitoring. This would establish an effect beyond individual protection and help assess claims about elimination.

uncertain: The levels of protection, duration, safety and dosing burden that would count as sufficient remain undefined.
It remains unclear whether genetic weakening can reliably preserve both safety and strong protection when used widely.

page.title: Malaria vaccine with 90% efficacy over 12 months
page.definition: A WHO-prequalified vaccine that reduces the incidence of all clinical malaria episodes by 90% over 12 months after immunization. Clinical malaria is symptomatic malaria confirmed by parasite detection under the study’s case definition.

goal.need: Children under 5 accounted for about 75% of malaria deaths in the WHO African Region in 2024. A 2019 RTS,S/AS01 extension study enrolled 3084 children aged 3–7 years; neither the three-dose nor four-dose schedule retained statistically significant efficacy against clinical malaria during the additional 3 years of follow-up.

figures.caption: WHO estimates of the global malaria burden in 2024
figures.note: These estimates cover all malaria, rather than vaccine-preventable cases alone.

statements.quote: An intensified focus is now needed on developing higher efficacy long-duration vaccines
statements.context: WHO strategic priorities for malaria vaccines.

statements.quote: with the goal of developing a second-generation product that can offer very high-level efficacy against malaria disease in young African children.
statements.context: Simon Draper describes combining the RH5.1 blood-stage vaccine candidate with approved liver-stage vaccines.

completion.title: A WHO-prequalified malaria vaccine achieves 90% clinical-malaria efficacy over 12 months.
completion.criterion: Demonstrate 90% efficacy against the incidence of all clinical malaria episodes over 12 months after immunization in the intended at-risk population, normally children aged 5 years and under. Obtain WHO prequalification for the same vaccine and intended use, including assessment of quality, safety, efficacy and programmatic suitability.
completion.set_by: World Health Organization, 2022 preferred product characteristics, section 2.2 and section 3.8. The numerical efficacy-duration preference appears in the table on printed page 10.
completion.basis: WHO’s 90% figure is a preferred development target, not a licensing minimum. Prequalification supplies an external assessment of the product and its suitability for immunization programmes.

milestones.title: A malaria vaccine passes nonclinical evaluation and gains authorization for a first human trial.
milestones.criterion: A regulator authorizes clinical testing after review of the candidate’s nonclinical package. In 2022, GA2 was evaluated in seven mice with human liver cells and red blood cells given 10^6 sporozoites, the parasite form injected by mosquitoes, with four wild-type controls. Cultures of day-9 blood remained negative for blood-stage parasites for 28 days. The GA2 preclinical package received clearance for human evaluation.
milestones.set_by: WHO nonclinical evaluation guidance; GA2 clinical clearance documented by Franke-Fayard and colleagues. The mouse experiment is evidence for GA2, not a universal numerical requirement.
milestones.threshold_quote: Non-clinical testing is a prerequisite to moving a candidate vaccine from the laboratory to the clinic

milestones.title: A malaria vaccine reaches first human dosing in an authorized clinical safety study.
milestones.criterion: Administer the candidate in an authorized preliminary human study exploring dose-related safety and immune responses. The GA2 study reported in 2024 enrolled 43 adults aged 19–35 years. Its 20-person dose-escalation stage used 15 or 50 infected mosquito bites and detected no breakthrough blood-stage infection by quantitative PCR. No serious adverse events occurred during the trial.
milestones.set_by: WHO Expert Committee on Biological Standardization, clinical evaluation guidelines, section 4.2.1. The GA2 study was authorized by the Dutch Central Committee for Research Involving Human Subjects.
milestones.threshold_quote: The clinical programme for new candidate vaccines usually commences with an exploration of the safety of different amounts of the antigen(s)

milestones.title: A malaria vaccine prevents or delays infection after controlled human malaria challenge.
milestones.criterion: Demonstrate prevention or delay of infection in controlled human malaria infection, a monitored deliberate exposure, using time to infection or the proportion remaining uninfected. Reported in 2024, GA2 protected 8/9 participants versus 0/3 placebo recipients against a matching-strain challenge 3 weeks after three 50-bite immunizations. Reported in 2025, one 50-bite immunization protected 9/10 participants versus 0/5 placebo recipients against a matching-strain challenge at 6 weeks.
milestones.set_by: World Health Organization, 2022 preferred product characteristics, section 3.7, proof-of-concept endpoints. WHO does not prescribe a universal minimum challenge efficacy.
milestones.threshold_quote: quantifying the proportion of participants who do not experience an infection.

milestones.title: A malaria vaccine’s phase 3 trial excludes a 30% lower efficacy limit over 12 months.
milestones.criterion: Meet the R21/Matrix-M protocol’s design objective of excluding a lower efficacy limit of 30% over 12 months at seasonal and standard sites, separately, in children aged 5–36 months. The primary endpoint is first clinical malaria from 14 days after dose three. Of 4878 children receiving a first dose, 4644 entered the modified per-protocol analysis. Reported in 2024, efficacy was 75% (95% CI 71–79) at seasonal sites and 68% (61–74) at standard sites; corresponding all-episode efficacy was 75% (71–78) and 67% (59–73).
milestones.set_by: University of Oxford, R21/Matrix-M phase 3 protocol NCT04704830, as described in the published trial. The 30% design bound belongs to this protocol, not to all malaria vaccine licensing decisions.
milestones.threshold_quote: to exclude a lower limit of efficacy of 30% if the vaccine efficacy was at least 50%.

milestones.title: A malaria vaccine receives national marketing authorization for its intended use.
milestones.criterion: Obtain national regulatory approval for the vaccine’s intended use. National registration precedes WHO prequalification. Ghana’s FDA reports approving R21 in 2023. WHO’s product registry records R21 prequalification effective 19 December 2023, intramuscular administration, and a 24-month shelf life at 2–8°C.
milestones.set_by: Ghana Food and Drugs Authority, R21 national approval documented in its 2023 Annual Report. WHO specifies national registration as a prerequisite for prequalification.
milestones.threshold_quote: The FDA became the first Regulatory Agency (ahead of WHO) to grant approval to the R21 Malaria vaccine.

not_found: No published study was found demonstrating the complete 90%-over-12-months profile in a WHO-prequalified malaria vaccine.
No universal numerical adverse-event ceiling or maximum dose count was found in WHO’s malaria vaccine guidance.

results.finding: GA2 protected 9 of 10 immunized participants against controlled malaria challenge.
results.detail: Participants received one immunization and underwent a homologous challenge six weeks later; none of five placebo recipients were protected.
results.quote: Here we report the safe administration of GA2-MB with no breakthrough malaria and sterile protection in nine of ten participants at 6 weeks after a single immunization with 50 GA2-infected mosquitoes, compared with none of five mock-immunized participants, against a homologous controlled human malaria infection.

results.finding: RTS,S/AS01 had 23.7% clinical-malaria efficacy over the entire follow-up among 1,739 older children enrolled in the extension.
results.detail: The phase 3 extension reports efficacy over approximately seven years, not the specified 12-month first-episode endpoint at seasonal and standard sites separately. Its 95% confidence interval was 15.9%–30.7%.
results.quote:

results.finding: In a 43-person GA2 trial, no serious adverse events occurred.
results.detail: The approved trial included a 20-person dose-escalation safety stage and assessed immune responses.

results.finding: GA2 protected 8 of 9 participants against controlled malaria infection.
results.detail: The matching-strain challenge occurred three weeks after three immunizations; 0 of 3 placebo recipients were protected.

results.finding: GA2 received regulatory approval for human testing after preclinical evaluation in 7 humanized mice.
results.detail: Day-9 blood cultures from the seven GA2-exposed mice remained negative for blood-stage parasites for 28 days. The paper reports Dutch regulatory and research committee approvals.

results.finding: PfSPZ-CVac(CQ) protected 6 of 6 participants against heterologous controlled human malaria infection.
results.detail: Challenge occurred three months after immunization. All 8 heterologous-challenge infectivity controls developed parasitaemia; participants were followed for up to 27 days.
results.quote:
At the higher dose, PfSPZ-CVac(CQ) protected six out of six 
(100%) participants against heterologous CHMI three months after immunization.

results.finding: R21/Matrix-M phase 3 trial (n=4644): 12-month efficacy lower confidence limits were 71% at seasonal sites and 61% at standard sites.
results.detail: The primary endpoint was time to first clinical malaria, beginning 14 days after dose three. Both site-specific lower limits exceed 30%.
results.quote: 12-month vaccine efficacy was 75% (95% CI 71–79; p<0·0001) at the seasonal sites and 68% (61–74; p<0·0001) at the standard sites for time to first clinical malaria episode.
